CHAPTER 27 - UNIVERSE

Introduction

When we look up at a clear night sky we see the Moon, a few planets, and thousands of stars. Beyond what the naked eye can see lies a universe of unimaginable size, filled with billions of stars grouped into galaxies, and vast stretches of nearly empty space. This chapter applies the physics you have already learnt - gravitation, nuclear fusion, the electromagnetic spectrum and the Doppler effect - to the largest objects and distances in nature. We begin close to home with the solar system, move outward to the Sun and the stars, follow how a star is born and dies, and finally consider the universe as a whole and how it began in the Big Bang.

27.1 THE SOLAR SYSTEM

The solar system consists of the Sun at the centre and everything gravitationally bound to it: eight planets, their moons, dwarf planets, asteroids, comets and meteoroids. The Sun contains about 99.8 percent of the total mass of the solar system, so its gravity controls the motion of all the other members. The eight planets, in order of increasing distance from the Sun, are Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune.
The first four (Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars) are the TERRESTRIAL or rocky planets - small, dense, with solid surfaces. The next four (Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune) are the JOVIAN or giant planets - large, gaseous, of low density; Saturn is famous for its bright ring system. The planets move around the Sun in elliptical orbits, obeying Kepler's laws, all roughly in the same plane and in the same direction.
Between the orbits of Mars and Jupiter lies the ASTEROID BELT, a region containing a large number of rocky bodies called asteroids (minor planets) ranging in size from a few metres to hundreds of kilometres. COMETS are small icy bodies that travel on highly elongated (eccentric) orbits. When a comet approaches the Sun the ice vaporises and forms a glowing head (coma) and a long tail that always points AWAY from the Sun, because it is pushed by the solar wind and radiation pressure. METEOROIDS are small pieces of rock or metal moving through space; when one enters the Earth's atmosphere it burns up by friction and appears as a bright streak of light called a METEOR (a shooting star). If a fragment survives and reaches the ground it is called a METEORITE.

27.2 THE SUN AND SOLAR ENERGY

The Sun is an ordinary star - a huge ball of hot gas (plasma) held together by its own gravity. Its main constituents are hydrogen (about 74 percent by mass) and helium (about 24 percent). Moving outward, the Sun has an internal structure: the CORE, where energy is generated; the RADIATIVE ZONE and the CONVECTIVE ZONE, through which energy travels outward; and the visible surface, the PHOTOSPHERE, at a temperature of about 5800 K. Above the photosphere lie the thin, hotter layers of the atmosphere - the CHROMOSPHERE and the CORONA (visible during a total solar eclipse). Dark, cooler patches on the photosphere are called SUNSPOTS.
Source of solar energy. The Sun radiates energy at an enormous rate (about 3.8 x 10^26 W) and has been doing so for billions of years. Chemical burning or gravitational contraction cannot supply this for so long. The true source is NUCLEAR FUSION in the core, where the temperature is about 1.5 x 10^7 K and the pressure is enormous. Four hydrogen nuclei (protons) combine, through a sequence of steps called the PROTON-PROTON CYCLE, to form one helium nucleus:
   4 (1H) -> (4He) + 2 positrons + 2 neutrinos + energy.
The helium nucleus is slightly LESS massive than the four protons that made it. This tiny mass difference (the mass defect, delta-m) is converted into energy according to Einstein's relation E = (delta-m) c^2. Because c^2 is a very large number, a small mass loss releases a huge amount of energy. This is why the Sun can shine for about ten billion years in total.
Solar constant. The SOLAR CONSTANT (S) is the amount of solar energy received per second per unit area on a surface held perpendicular to the Sun's rays, just outside the Earth's atmosphere, at the mean Earth-Sun distance. Its value is about S = 1.36 x 10^3 W/m^2 (roughly 1.36 kW per square metre). From the solar constant one can estimate the Sun's total power output (luminosity): imagine a huge sphere of radius equal to the Earth-Sun distance r; the whole output passes through it, so Luminosity L = S x 4 pi r^2. Putting r = 1.5 x 10^11 m gives about 3.8 x 10^26 W.

27.3 ASTRONOMICAL DISTANCES AND STARS

Distances in astronomy are far too large for metres or kilometres to be convenient, so special units are used.
 - ASTRONOMICAL UNIT (AU): the mean distance between the Earth and the Sun, 1 AU = 1.496 x 10^11 m (about 1.5 x 10^11 m). Used for distances within the solar system.
 - LIGHT YEAR (ly): the distance light travels in one year in vacuum. Since light travels at c = 3 x 10^8 m/s, 1 ly = c x (1 year in seconds) = (3 x 10^8) x (3.156 x 10^7) = about 9.46 x 10^15 m. Note a light year is a unit of DISTANCE, not time. The nearest star (Proxima Centauri) is about 4.2 ly away.
 - PARSEC (pc): the distance at which 1 AU subtends an angle of 1 arc-second (1/3600 of a degree). 1 pc = 3.086 x 10^16 m = 3.26 ly. The parsec is defined through stellar PARALLAX - the tiny apparent shift of a nearby star against the distant background as the Earth moves around the Sun. A star at distance d parsec shows a parallax angle p arc-seconds where d = 1 / p.
Stars: brightness, magnitude and luminosity. Stars differ in how bright they appear and in how much energy they actually emit. The APPARENT BRIGHTNESS (or apparent magnitude) is how bright a star looks from Earth; it depends both on the star's true output and on its distance. The MAGNITUDE scale is reversed and logarithmic: a SMALLER (or more negative) magnitude means a BRIGHTER star. The LUMINOSITY of a star is the total energy it radiates per second - its true power output, a property of the star itself. A nearby dim-looking star may actually be more luminous than a bright-looking distant one; brightness falls off as 1/(distance)^2.
The colour of a star indicates its surface temperature: blue-white stars are the hottest, yellow stars (like the Sun) are of moderate temperature, and red stars are the coolest. The HERTZSPRUNG-RUSSELL (H-R) DIAGRAM is a graph of luminosity (vertical axis) against surface temperature or colour (horizontal axis, plotted with temperature decreasing to the right). Most stars, including the Sun, lie along a diagonal band called the MAIN SEQUENCE, running from hot-luminous stars at the top left to cool-faint stars at the bottom right. Away from the main sequence lie the cool but very luminous RED GIANTS (top right) and the hot but faint WHITE DWARFS (bottom left). The H-R diagram is a powerful tool for understanding how stars evolve.

27.4 STELLAR EVOLUTION

A star is born, lives and dies. The stages depend mainly on the star's MASS.
Birth. Stars form inside cold clouds of gas and dust called NEBULAE. Under its own gravity a dense clump contracts, heats up, and forms a PROTOSTAR. When the core becomes hot enough (about 10^7 K) hydrogen fusion begins, and a stable star is born.
Main sequence. For most of its life the star fuses hydrogen into helium in its core. During this long, stable phase the inward pull of gravity is exactly balanced by the outward pressure of the hot gas and radiation - a state called HYDROSTATIC EQUILIBRIUM. The Sun is in this phase now. More massive stars burn their fuel faster and so have SHORTER lifetimes.
Red giant. When the hydrogen in the core runs out, the core contracts and heats while the outer layers expand and cool, so the star swells into a RED GIANT (or a red supergiant for very massive stars). Fusion of helium into heavier elements such as carbon can now occur in the core.
Death of a low-mass star. A star like the Sun cannot fuse elements beyond carbon. Its outer layers are gently blown off as a glowing shell (a planetary nebula), leaving behind the hot, dense core - a WHITE DWARF, about the size of the Earth but with a mass comparable to the Sun. A white dwarf slowly cools and fades over billions of years.
The Chandrasekhar limit. A white dwarf is supported against gravity by ELECTRON DEGENERACY PRESSURE. There is a maximum mass a white dwarf can have, the CHANDRASEKHAR LIMIT, equal to about 1.4 times the mass of the Sun. A stellar remnant more massive than this cannot survive as a white dwarf; gravity crushes it further.
Death of a massive star. A star much heavier than the Sun fuses successively heavier elements up to IRON in its core. Iron cannot release energy on fusing, so the core collapses catastrophically in less than a second and the outer layers rebound in a colossal explosion - a SUPERNOVA - which for a few days can outshine an entire galaxy and which scatters heavy elements into space. What remains of the core depends on its mass: if between about 1.4 and 3 solar masses it becomes an extremely dense NEUTRON STAR (a fast-spinning neutron star seen as a pulsar); if more massive still, nothing can halt the collapse and it becomes a BLACK HOLE - a region whose gravity is so strong that not even light can escape from within its event horizon.

27.5 GALAXIES AND THE MILKY WAY

Stars are not spread uniformly through space; they are gathered into enormous systems called GALAXIES, each held together by gravity and containing anywhere from millions to hundreds of billions of stars, along with gas, dust and dark matter. Our own galaxy is the MILKY WAY, a SPIRAL galaxy containing roughly 100 to 400 billion stars and about 100000 light years across. The Sun lies in one of its spiral arms, about 27000 light years from the centre, and takes roughly 250 million years to orbit the galactic centre once. On a dark night the combined light of the galaxy's distant stars appears as a faint milky band across the sky - this is how the Milky Way gets its name.
Galaxies come in several shapes. Edwin Hubble classified them as SPIRAL galaxies (a central bulge with winding arms, like the Milky Way and the Andromeda galaxy), ELLIPTICAL galaxies (smooth, featureless ellipsoids of mostly old stars) and IRREGULAR galaxies (no definite shape). Galaxies themselves cluster together into groups and clusters, and clusters into still larger superclusters - the largest known structures in the universe. Andromeda, the nearest large galaxy to ours, is about 2.5 million light years away.

27.6 THE EXPANDING UNIVERSE AND THE BIG BANG

In the 1920s Edwin Hubble measured the distances to many galaxies and, using the DOPPLER EFFECT, their velocities. The light from almost every galaxy is shifted toward the red (longer-wavelength) end of the spectrum - a REDSHIFT - showing that the galaxies are moving AWAY from us. Hubble found a simple relation: the greater the distance to a galaxy, the faster it is receding. This is HUBBLE'S LAW:
   v = H0 x d,
where v is the recession velocity, d is the distance to the galaxy, and H0 is HUBBLE'S CONSTANT (about 70 km/s per megaparsec). The universe is EXPANDING: every galaxy sees all the others moving away, not because we are at a special centre, but because space itself is stretching, carrying the galaxies apart like raisins in a rising loaf of bread.
Running the expansion backwards in time, everything must once have been packed together at enormous density and temperature. This is the BIG BANG theory: about 13.8 billion years ago the universe began in an extremely hot, dense state and has been expanding and cooling ever since. The value 1/H0 gives a rough estimate of the age of the universe.
Evidence for the Big Bang.
 (1) The EXPANSION itself (Hubble's law) - galaxies receding, exactly as an expanding universe requires.
 (2) The COSMIC MICROWAVE BACKGROUND (CMB): a faint microwave radiation coming almost uniformly from every direction in the sky, discovered by Penzias and Wilson in 1965. It is the cooled-down afterglow of the hot early universe, now at a temperature of only about 2.7 K - a direct relic of the Big Bang.
 (3) The observed ABUNDANCE of the light elements - about 75 percent hydrogen and 25 percent helium by mass, plus traces of lithium - matches exactly what nuclear reactions in the first few minutes after the Big Bang (nucleosynthesis) predict.
Dark matter and dark energy. The motions of stars in galaxies and of galaxies in clusters are far faster than the visible matter's gravity can explain. Astronomers conclude that most of the matter in the universe is invisible DARK MATTER, which we detect only through its gravity. Furthermore, observations show that the expansion of the universe is not slowing down but ACCELERATING; the cause is attributed to a mysterious DARK ENERGY that fills space and acts as a kind of repulsion. Ordinary matter (stars, planets, gas) makes up only about 5 percent of the universe; dark matter about 27 percent and dark energy about 68 percent. What most of the universe is made of thus remains one of the great open questions of physics.

WORKED EXAMPLES

Example 1 (Hubble's law). A galaxy is at a distance of 100 Mpc. Taking H0 = 70 km/s per Mpc, find its recession velocity.
   v = H0 x d = 70 x 100 = 7000 km/s. The galaxy is receding at about 7000 km/s.

Example 2 (Hubble's law, reversed). A galaxy recedes at 21000 km/s. With H0 = 70 km/s/Mpc, how far away is it?
   d = v / H0 = 21000 / 70 = 300 Mpc.

Example 3 (distance-unit conversion). Express 1 parsec in light years, given 1 pc = 3.086 x 10^16 m and 1 ly = 9.46 x 10^15 m.
   1 pc = (3.086 x 10^16) / (9.46 x 10^15) ly = 3.26 ly.

Example 4 (light year). How far does light travel in 4.2 years (the distance to Proxima Centauri)?
   distance = 4.2 ly = 4.2 x 9.46 x 10^15 m = about 3.97 x 10^16 m.

Example 5 (mass-energy). If 4 x 10^9 kg of matter is converted to energy each second in a star, estimate the power released. Using E = m c^2 with c = 3 x 10^8 m/s: P = (4 x 10^9) x (3 x 10^8)^2 = 4 x 10^9 x 9 x 10^16 = 3.6 x 10^26 W, comparable to the Sun's luminosity.

SUMMARY

- The solar system is the Sun plus eight planets (four rocky terrestrial, four gaseous Jovian), moons, asteroids (mostly between Mars and Jupiter), comets (icy, with tails pointing away from the Sun) and meteoroids (seen as meteors when they burn in the atmosphere).
- The Sun is a star made mainly of hydrogen and helium; its energy comes from nuclear fusion of hydrogen into helium (the proton-proton cycle), the mass defect being released as energy via E = (delta-m) c^2. The solar constant is about 1.36 kW/m^2.
- Astronomical distances use the AU (Earth-Sun distance, 1.5 x 10^11 m), the light year (9.46 x 10^15 m) and the parsec (3.086 x 10^16 m = 3.26 ly). Parsec is defined through stellar parallax, d(pc) = 1 / p(arc-second).
- A star's apparent brightness depends on distance; its luminosity is its true output. On the magnitude scale a smaller number is brighter. The H-R diagram plots luminosity against temperature; most stars lie on the main sequence.
- Stellar evolution: nebula -> protostar -> main sequence -> red giant -> (low mass) white dwarf, or (high mass) supernova leaving a neutron star or black hole. The Chandrasekhar limit (about 1.4 solar masses) is the maximum mass of a white dwarf.
- Stars group into galaxies (spiral, elliptical, irregular). Our Milky Way is a spiral galaxy about 100000 ly across.
- The universe is expanding: Hubble's law v = H0 d, seen as galaxy redshifts. Extrapolating back gives the Big Bang (about 13.8 billion years ago). Evidence: expansion, the 2.7 K cosmic microwave background, and the abundance of light elements. Most of the universe is dark matter and dark energy.

questions.question: Distinguish between a meteoroid, a meteor and a meteorite.
questions.answer: A METEOROID is a small piece of rock or metal moving through space. When such a body enters the Earth's atmosphere it burns up by friction and appears as a bright streak of light - this streak is a METEOR (a shooting star). If a fragment survives the passage through the atmosphere and reaches the ground, that surviving piece is called a METEORITE.
questions.explanation: The three terms refer to the same kind of object at three stages: in space, burning in the air, and landed.

questions.question: Explain how nuclear fusion supplies the Sun's energy, and why chemical burning cannot.
questions.answer: In the Sun's core (about 1.5 x 10^7 K) four hydrogen nuclei fuse through the proton-proton cycle into one helium nucleus. The helium nucleus is slightly less massive than the four protons; this mass defect (delta-m) is converted to energy by E = (delta-m) c^2. Because c^2 is enormous, even a tiny mass loss releases a huge amount of energy, enough to power the Sun for about ten billion years. Chemical burning releases only a few electron-volts per reaction, far too little to sustain the Sun's output (3.8 x 10^26 W) for billions of years - the Sun would have burnt out long ago.
questions.explanation: Fusion converts mass to energy via E=mc^2, releasing millions of times more energy per reaction than chemistry.

questions.question: A galaxy lies at a distance of 150 Mpc. Taking H0 = 70 km/s per Mpc, calculate its recession velocity using Hubble's law.
questions.answer: Hubble's law: v = H0 x d = 70 x 150 = 10500 km/s. The galaxy is receding at about 1.05 x 10^4 km/s (10500 km/s).
questions.explanation: Direct substitution into v = H0 d with d in Mpc and H0 in km/s/Mpc.

questions.question: Express 1 parsec in (a) metres and (b) light years. Given 1 pc = 3.086 x 10^16 m and 1 ly = 9.46 x 10^15 m.
questions.answer: (a) By definition 1 pc = 3.086 x 10^16 m. (b) 1 pc in light years = (3.086 x 10^16) / (9.46 x 10^15) = 3.26 ly. So one parsec equals about 3.086 x 10^16 m or 3.26 light years.
questions.explanation: Divide the parsec (in m) by the light year (in m) to convert.

questions.question: Trace the life cycle of a low-mass star like the Sun and that of a massive star (about 20 solar masses), naming the final remnant in each case and explaining what decides it.
questions.answer:
Both start the same way: a cold cloud of gas and dust (a NEBULA) contracts under gravity into a hot PROTOSTAR, and when the core reaches about 10^7 K hydrogen fusion begins - the star joins the MAIN SEQUENCE, where gravity is balanced by outward pressure. When the core hydrogen is exhausted the star swells into a RED GIANT (or supergiant).
Low-mass star (Sun): it cannot fuse elements beyond carbon. Its outer layers drift off as a planetary nebula, leaving the hot dense core as a WHITE DWARF (Earth-sized, ~1 solar mass), supported by electron degeneracy pressure, which slowly cools and fades.
Massive star (~20 M_sun): it fuses successively heavier elements up to IRON. Iron fusion absorbs rather than releases energy, so the core collapses in under a second and the outer layers rebound in a SUPERNOVA. The remnant left behind depends on the core mass: between about 1.4 and 3 solar masses it becomes a NEUTRON STAR; above that, gravity wins completely and it forms a BLACK HOLE.
The deciding factor is MASS. The Chandrasekhar limit (~1.4 M_sun) is the maximum mass a white dwarf can have; more massive cores are crushed into neutron stars or black holes.
questions.explanation: Common early stages, then mass determines white dwarf vs neutron star vs black hole; the Chandrasekhar limit is the key threshold.

questions.question: State Hubble's law and explain what it tells us about the universe.
questions.answer: Hubble's law states that a galaxy's recession velocity is proportional to its distance: v = H0 x d, where H0 is Hubble's constant (about 70 km/s per megaparsec). It tells us that almost all galaxies are moving away from us and that the farther a galaxy is, the faster it recedes. This means the universe is EXPANDING - space itself is stretching and carrying galaxies apart - and it implies that in the past everything was closer together, pointing back to the Big Bang.
questions.explanation: v = H0 d; proportionality of recession to distance implies uniform expansion of space.

questions.question: What is the solar constant? A surface of area 2 m^2 faces the Sun just outside the atmosphere. How much solar energy does it receive in 1 second? (Take S = 1.36 x 10^3 W/m^2.)
questions.answer: The SOLAR CONSTANT is the amount of solar energy received per second per unit area, on a surface held perpendicular to the Sun's rays just outside the Earth's atmosphere, at the mean Earth-Sun distance; its value is about 1.36 x 10^3 W/m^2. Energy per second on 2 m^2 = S x area = 1.36 x 10^3 x 2 = 2.72 x 10^3 W, i.e. 2720 joules in 1 second.
questions.explanation: Multiply the solar constant by the area to get power received.

questions.question: The light from distant galaxies is redshifted. What is a redshift and what does it indicate?
questions.answer: A REDSHIFT is a shift of the lines in a galaxy's spectrum toward the longer-wavelength (red) end. By the Doppler effect, light from a source moving away from us is stretched to longer wavelengths. So the redshift of nearly all galaxies indicates that they are moving AWAY from us - evidence that the universe is expanding. A larger redshift means a greater recession velocity and (by Hubble's law) a greater distance.
questions.explanation: Doppler stretching of light from a receding source; near-universal redshift shows cosmic expansion.

questions.question: Describe the Big Bang theory and give three independent lines of observational evidence that support it.
questions.answer:
The BIG BANG theory holds that about 13.8 billion years ago the universe began in an extremely hot, dense state and has been expanding and cooling ever since. Three lines of evidence support it:
(1) THE EXPANSION OF THE UNIVERSE. Hubble's law (v = H0 d) shows galaxies receding, with speed proportional to distance - exactly what a uniformly expanding universe requires. Running the expansion backward, everything was once packed together.
(2) THE COSMIC MICROWAVE BACKGROUND (CMB). A faint microwave radiation of temperature about 2.7 K reaches us almost equally from every direction (discovered by Penzias and Wilson, 1965). It is the cooled-down afterglow of the hot early universe - a direct relic of the Big Bang.
(3) THE ABUNDANCE OF LIGHT ELEMENTS. The universe is about 75 percent hydrogen and 25 percent helium by mass, with traces of lithium. These proportions match precisely what nuclear reactions (nucleosynthesis) in the first few minutes after the Big Bang predict.
Together these three independent observations make the Big Bang the accepted description of the origin of the universe.
questions.explanation: Definition plus the three standard pieces of evidence: expansion, CMB, and light-element abundances.

questions.question: Distinguish between the apparent brightness (magnitude) and the luminosity of a star.
questions.answer: The LUMINOSITY of a star is the total energy it radiates per second - its true power output, a fixed property of the star itself. The APPARENT BRIGHTNESS (apparent magnitude) is how bright the star looks from Earth; it depends both on the luminosity and on the distance, because brightness falls off as 1/(distance)^2. Thus a very luminous star that is far away can look fainter than a much less luminous star that is nearby. On the magnitude scale a smaller (or more negative) number means a brighter-looking star.
questions.explanation: Luminosity is intrinsic; apparent brightness also depends on distance via the inverse-square law.

questions.question: Distinguish between terrestrial and Jovian planets, giving one example of each.

questions.question: What is a comet, and why does it develop a tail near the Sun?
questions.answer: A comet is a small icy body that orbits the Sun on a highly elongated path. As it nears the Sun the ice vaporises, forming a glowing head (coma) and a long tail. The tail is pushed by the solar wind and radiation pressure, so it always points away from the Sun.

questions.question: Describe the main layers of the Sun from the centre outward.
questions.answer: From the centre outward: the CORE, where fusion generates energy; the RADIATIVE ZONE, through which energy travels as radiation; the CONVECTIVE ZONE, where hot gas carries energy by convection; the PHOTOSPHERE, the visible surface (~5800 K); and above it the thin CHROMOSPHERE and the outer CORONA (seen during a total eclipse).
questions.explanation: Core, radiative zone, convective zone, photosphere, chromosphere, corona.

questions.question: Explain the role of the mass defect in producing the Sun's energy.
questions.answer: When four hydrogen nuclei fuse into one helium nucleus, the helium nucleus is slightly less massive than the four protons. This small missing mass is the MASS DEFECT (delta-m). It is converted into energy according to E = (delta-m) c^2. Because c^2 is very large, even a tiny mass loss releases an enormous amount of energy, which is what the Sun radiates.
questions.explanation: The missing mass in fusion becomes energy via E = (delta-m)c^2.

questions.question: Name the source of the Sun's energy and the nuclei involved.
questions.answer: The source is NUCLEAR FUSION in the core. Hydrogen nuclei (protons) fuse, through the proton-proton cycle, into helium nuclei, releasing energy.
questions.explanation: Fusion of hydrogen into helium.

questions.question: Define the solar constant and state its approximate value.
questions.answer: The SOLAR CONSTANT is the amount of solar energy received per second per unit area on a surface held perpendicular to the Sun's rays, just outside the Earth's atmosphere, at the mean Earth-Sun distance. Its value is about 1.36 x 10^3 W/m^2 (about 1.36 kW/m^2).

questions.question: The solar constant is 1.36 x 10^3 W/m^2 and the Earth-Sun distance is 1.5 x 10^11 m. Estimate the Sun's luminosity. (Take 4 pi = 12.57.)

questions.question: Two stars look equally bright, but one is much farther than the other. What can you say about their luminosities?
questions.answer: Apparent brightness depends on both luminosity and distance, falling off as 1/(distance)^2. If two stars look equally bright but one is much farther away, the more distant star must be far more LUMINOUS (emitting much more energy per second) to appear as bright despite its greater distance. The nearer one is intrinsically fainter.
questions.explanation: Equal brightness at greater distance implies greater luminosity (inverse-square law).

questions.question: What does the H-R diagram plot, and where do most stars lie on it?
questions.answer: The Hertzsprung-Russell (H-R) diagram plots the LUMINOSITY of stars (vertical axis) against their SURFACE TEMPERATURE or colour (horizontal axis, with temperature decreasing to the right). Most stars, including the Sun, lie along a diagonal band called the MAIN SEQUENCE.
questions.explanation: Luminosity vs temperature; most stars lie on the main sequence.

questions.question: What is meant by the main sequence in a star's life?
questions.answer: The main sequence is the long, stable phase in which a star fuses hydrogen into helium in its core. During this phase the inward pull of gravity is balanced by the outward pressure of hot gas and radiation (hydrostatic equilibrium). A star spends most of its life on the main sequence; the Sun is in this phase now.
questions.explanation: The stable hydrogen-burning phase where most of a star's life is spent.

questions.question: Explain why a star more massive than about 3 solar masses in its core can end as a black hole, while a Sun-like star cannot.
questions.answer: The final state of a star is set by the mass of the remnant left after it dies. A Sun-like star sheds its outer layers and leaves a core below the Chandrasekhar limit (~1.4 M_sun); electron degeneracy pressure supports it as a WHITE DWARF. A very massive star explodes as a supernova; if the leftover core exceeds about 3 solar masses, no known pressure can resist gravity, so the core collapses without limit into a BLACK HOLE. A Sun-like star simply never has enough mass in its remnant for this to happen.
questions.explanation: Remnant mass decides the fate; above ~3 M_sun gravity forms a black hole.

questions.question: What is a supernova and why is it important for the chemistry of the universe?
questions.answer: A supernova is the colossal explosion of a massive star at the end of its life, briefly outshining an entire galaxy. It is important because it scatters heavy elements (formed inside the star and in the explosion) into space, enriching the gas from which new stars and planets - and ultimately living things - are made.
questions.explanation: Explosive death of a massive star that disperses heavy elements.

questions.question: State what the Chandrasekhar limit is and its approximate value.
questions.answer: The Chandrasekhar limit is the maximum mass that a white dwarf can have; it is about 1.4 times the mass of the Sun. A stellar remnant more massive than this cannot be supported by electron degeneracy pressure and collapses further into a neutron star or black hole.
questions.explanation: Maximum white-dwarf mass, ~1.4 solar masses.

questions.question: Describe the Milky Way and the Sun's location within it.
questions.answer: The Milky Way is a SPIRAL galaxy containing roughly 100 to 400 billion stars and about 100000 light years across. The Sun lies in one of its spiral arms, about 27000 light years from the galactic centre, and takes roughly 250 million years to orbit the centre once.
questions.explanation: Spiral galaxy ~100000 ly across; Sun in a spiral arm ~27000 ly from centre.

questions.question: State Hubble's classification of galaxies with a brief description of each type.
questions.answer: Edwin Hubble classified galaxies into three main types: SPIRAL galaxies, which have a central bulge with winding arms (like the Milky Way and Andromeda); ELLIPTICAL galaxies, which are smooth, featureless ellipsoids of mostly old stars; and IRREGULAR galaxies, which have no definite shape.
questions.explanation: Spiral, elliptical and irregular galaxies.

questions.question: State two lines of evidence for the Big Bang and explain each briefly.
questions.answer: (1) THE EXPANSION OF THE UNIVERSE: Hubble's law shows galaxies receding with speed proportional to distance, as an expanding universe requires; running this backward implies a dense hot origin. (2) THE COSMIC MICROWAVE BACKGROUND: a faint 2.7 K microwave radiation from all directions, the cooled afterglow of the hot early universe. (A third line is the observed 75:25 hydrogen-to-helium abundance predicted by Big Bang nucleosynthesis.)
questions.explanation: Expansion (Hubble's law) and the 2.7 K cosmic microwave background.

questions.question: What are dark matter and dark energy, and why are they proposed?
questions.answer: DARK MATTER is invisible matter detected only through its gravity; it is proposed because stars in galaxies and galaxies in clusters move faster than the gravity of the visible matter can explain. DARK ENERGY is a mysterious form of energy filling space that acts like a repulsion; it is proposed because the expansion of the universe is observed to be accelerating rather than slowing. Together they make up about 95 percent of the universe.
questions.explanation: Dark matter explains extra gravity; dark energy explains accelerating expansion.

questions.question: A galaxy recedes at 7000 km/s. Using H0 = 70 km/s per Mpc, find its distance.
questions.answer: By Hubble's law, d = v / H0 = 7000 / 70 = 100 Mpc. The galaxy is about 100 megaparsec away.
questions.explanation: Rearrange v = H0 d to d = v/H0.

questions.question: Explain how Hubble's constant can be used to estimate the age of the universe, and give a rough idea of that age.
questions.answer: Hubble's law is v = H0 d. If a galaxy has always moved at speed v, the time taken to reach distance d is t = d/v = 1/H0. This reciprocal of Hubble's constant gives a rough estimate of the time since all galaxies were together - i.e. the age of the universe. Using H0 about 70 km/s/Mpc gives an age of roughly 13 to 14 billion years, consistent with the accepted value of about 13.8 billion years.
questions.explanation: Age ~ 1/H0, giving about 13.8 billion years.

questions.question: Describe the main members of the solar system.
questions.answer: The solar system consists of the SUN at the centre and everything bound to it by gravity. The Sun holds about 99.8 percent of the total mass. Around it move EIGHT PLANETS in elliptical orbits: the four inner TERRESTRIAL planets (Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars), which are small, dense and rocky; and the four outer JOVIAN giants (Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune), which are large, gaseous and of low density, Saturn being noted for its rings. Many planets have MOONS orbiting them. Between Mars and Jupiter lies the ASTEROID BELT, containing many rocky minor planets. COMETS are small icy bodies on elongated orbits that grow a tail (pointing away from the Sun) when they approach it. METEOROIDS are small rocky or metallic fragments; when one burns up in Earth's atmosphere it is seen as a METEOR, and any piece that lands is a METEORITE.
questions.explanation: Sun, planets (terrestrial and Jovian), moons, asteroids, comets, meteoroids.

questions.question: Explain in detail how the Sun produces its energy and why this source can last for billions of years.
questions.answer: The Sun radiates energy at about 3.8 x 10^26 W and has done so for billions of years. Chemical burning or gravitational contraction cannot supply this for so long. The true source is NUCLEAR FUSION in the core, where the temperature is about 1.5 x 10^7 K and the pressure is enormous. There, through the PROTON-PROTON CYCLE, four hydrogen nuclei fuse in a sequence of steps to form one helium nucleus, releasing positrons, neutrinos and energy: 4(1H) -> 4He + energy. The helium nucleus is slightly LESS massive than the four protons; this MASS DEFECT (delta-m) is converted to energy by Einstein's relation E = (delta-m) c^2. Because c^2 = 9 x 10^16 m^2/s^2 is very large, a tiny mass loss yields an enormous energy. The Sun has a vast store of hydrogen; converting even a small fraction of it releases enough energy to shine for about ten billion years in total. This is why fusion, unlike chemical burning, can power the Sun over cosmological timescales.
questions.explanation: Fusion (proton-proton cycle) converts mass to energy via E=mc^2; the huge hydrogen store lasts billions of years.

questions.question: Explain the three units of astronomical distance (AU, light year, parsec) and how they are related, with the value of each.
questions.answer:
Astronomical distances are too large for metres, so special units are used.
(1) ASTRONOMICAL UNIT (AU): the mean Earth-Sun distance, 1 AU = 1.496 x 10^11 m (about 1.5 x 10^11 m). It is convenient for distances within the solar system.
(2) LIGHT YEAR (ly): the distance light travels in one year in vacuum. With c = 3 x 10^8 m/s and 1 year = 3.156 x 10^7 s, 1 ly = 9.46 x 10^15 m. It is a unit of distance, not time; the nearest star is about 4.2 ly away.
(3) PARSEC (pc): the distance at which 1 AU subtends an angle of 1 arc-second. 1 pc = 3.086 x 10^16 m = 3.26 ly. It is defined through stellar parallax: a star at distance d parsec shows a parallax angle p arc-seconds with d = 1/p.
Relations: 1 pc = 3.26 ly = 206265 AU. Thus the parsec is the largest of the three, the light year next, and the AU the smallest, each suited to a different scale - solar system (AU), nearby stars (ly), and professional astronomy (pc).
questions.explanation: AU (Earth-Sun), light year (distance light travels in a year), parsec (parallax); 1 pc = 3.26 ly = 206265 AU.

questions.question: Compare the evolution and final states of a low-mass star and a high-mass star, explaining the role of mass.
questions.answer:
Both a low-mass star (like the Sun) and a high-mass star begin in a NEBULA that contracts into a PROTOSTAR and, once fusion starts, joins the MAIN SEQUENCE, where gravity is balanced by pressure. The difference lies in how they end, which is decided by MASS.
Low-mass star: after the core hydrogen is exhausted it swells into a RED GIANT and can fuse helium into carbon, but no further. It then sheds its outer layers as a planetary nebula, leaving a hot dense core - a WHITE DWARF - supported by electron degeneracy pressure, which slowly cools. A white dwarf cannot exceed the CHANDRASEKHAR LIMIT of about 1.4 solar masses.
High-mass star: it becomes a red supergiant and fuses elements successively up to IRON. Iron fusion absorbs energy, so the core collapses in under a second and the star explodes as a SUPERNOVA. The remnant depends on mass: about 1.4 to 3 solar masses gives a NEUTRON STAR (seen as a pulsar); above about 3 solar masses gravity is unstoppable and a BLACK HOLE forms.
Thus mass is the master variable: it fixes the lifetime (massive stars live shorter) and the final remnant - white dwarf, neutron star or black hole.
questions.explanation: Common early stages; mass decides white dwarf (< Chandrasekhar limit) vs neutron star vs black hole.

questions.question: Describe what galaxies are, how they are classified, and give the main features of the Milky Way.
questions.answer:
GALAXIES are enormous gravitationally bound systems of stars, gas, dust and dark matter, each containing from millions to hundreds of billions of stars. Edwin Hubble classified them by shape into three main types: SPIRAL galaxies (a central bulge with winding arms), ELLIPTICAL galaxies (smooth ellipsoids of mostly old stars) and IRREGULAR galaxies (no definite shape). Galaxies themselves gather into groups, clusters and superclusters - the largest structures in the universe.
Our own galaxy, the MILKY WAY, is a spiral galaxy about 100000 light years across containing roughly 100 to 400 billion stars. The Sun lies in one of its spiral arms, about 27000 light years from the centre, and orbits the galactic centre once in about 250 million years. Seen from inside, the disc of the galaxy appears as the faint milky band of light that crosses the night sky and gives the galaxy its name. The nearest large galaxy to ours is Andromeda, about 2.5 million light years away.
questions.explanation: Galaxies = bound star systems; spiral/elliptical/irregular; Milky Way is a spiral ~100000 ly across.

questions.question: State the Big Bang theory and discuss the evidence supporting it, including a brief mention of dark matter and dark energy.
questions.answer:
The BIG BANG theory states that about 13.8 billion years ago the universe began in an extremely hot, dense state and has been expanding and cooling ever since. The evidence:
(1) EXPANSION: Hubble's law v = H0 d shows galaxies receding, faster with greater distance, exactly as an expanding universe requires; extrapolating back, all matter was once together.
(2) COSMIC MICROWAVE BACKGROUND: a faint microwave radiation at about 2.7 K reaching us nearly equally from all directions (Penzias and Wilson, 1965) - the cooled afterglow of the hot early universe.
(3) LIGHT-ELEMENT ABUNDANCE: the universe is about 75 percent hydrogen and 25 percent helium by mass, matching the predictions of nuclear reactions in the first few minutes after the Big Bang.
Beyond ordinary matter, the motions of stars and galaxies reveal much unseen DARK MATTER (about 27 percent of the universe), detected only by its gravity, and the accelerating expansion is attributed to DARK ENERGY (about 68 percent). Ordinary matter is only about 5 percent. So while the Big Bang is well supported, most of the universe's content remains mysterious.
questions.explanation: Big Bang (~13.8 Gyr); evidence: expansion, CMB, light elements; dark matter and dark energy dominate.

questions.question: Explain Hubble's law and use it to work out (a) the recession velocity of a galaxy at 250 Mpc and (b) the distance of a galaxy receding at 4200 km/s. Take H0 = 70 km/s per Mpc.
questions.answer:
Hubble's law states that a galaxy's recession velocity is proportional to its distance: v = H0 d, where H0 (Hubble's constant) is about 70 km/s per megaparsec. It expresses the expansion of the universe - the farther a galaxy, the faster it recedes.
(a) v = H0 x d = 70 x 250 = 17500 km/s. The galaxy recedes at about 1.75 x 10^4 km/s.
(b) d = v / H0 = 4200 / 70 = 60 Mpc. The galaxy is about 60 megaparsec away.
The same law, run backward (t = 1/H0), also gives a rough age of the universe of about 13.8 billion years.

questions.question: Show how the solar constant leads to the Sun's luminosity, and separately estimate how much mass the Sun converts to energy each second. (Take S = 1.36 x 10^3 W/m^2, r = 1.5 x 10^11 m, c = 3 x 10^8 m/s, 4 pi = 12.57.)
questions.answer:
Luminosity from the solar constant: the Sun's entire output crosses a sphere of radius r equal to the Earth-Sun distance. Its area is 4 pi r^2 = 12.57 x (1.5 x 10^11)^2 = 12.57 x 2.25 x 10^22 = 2.83 x 10^23 m^2. So the luminosity L = S x 4 pi r^2 = 1.36 x 10^3 x 2.83 x 10^23 = about 3.8 x 10^26 W.
Mass converted per second: by E = m c^2, the mass turned into energy each second is m = L / c^2 = (3.8 x 10^26) / (9 x 10^16) = about 4.2 x 10^9 kg. So the Sun converts roughly four million tonnes of matter into energy every second, yet its huge mass lets it do so for billions of years.
questions.explanation: L = S x 4 pi r^2 = 3.8 x 10^26 W; mass/s = L/c^2 = about 4.2 x 10^9 kg.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
On a clear August night many people watch a 'meteor shower', when several bright streaks flash across the sky each hour. These streaks occur when tiny fragments left behind by a comet enter the Earth's atmosphere at high speed. Most burn up completely far above the ground; only rarely does a larger piece survive to land.
(a) What is the correct name for the bright streak seen in the sky?
(b) What causes the fragment to glow and burn?
(c) What do we call a piece that survives and reaches the ground?
(d) Name the type of body whose debris often causes such showers.
questions.answer: (a) The streak is a METEOR (a shooting star). (b) Friction with the air as the fragment moves at high speed heats it until it glows and burns up. (c) A surviving piece that lands is a METEORITE. (d) The debris often comes from a COMET, which leaves a trail of icy and rocky particles along its orbit.
questions.explanation: Meteor = streak; friction heats it; meteorite = landed piece; comets supply the debris.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
The Sun has shone steadily for about 4.6 billion years. Its core is at about 15 million kelvin, where hydrogen is converted into helium. The helium produced has slightly less mass than the hydrogen that formed it, and this missing mass appears as energy.
(a) Name the process occurring in the Sun's core.
(b) Write the relation connecting the missing mass and the energy released.
(c) Why can this process last for billions of years while chemical burning cannot?
(d) Name the visible surface of the Sun.
questions.answer: (a) The process is NUCLEAR FUSION (the proton-proton cycle), fusing hydrogen into helium. (b) E = (delta-m) c^2, where delta-m is the mass defect. (c) Fusion releases millions of times more energy per reaction than chemistry because c^2 is huge, and the Sun has an enormous store of hydrogen, so it can last billions of years; chemical burning releases far too little energy to sustain the Sun for so long. (d) The visible surface is the PHOTOSPHERE.
questions.explanation: Fusion; E=(delta-m)c^2; huge energy per reaction plus vast fuel; photosphere.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
Just outside the Earth's atmosphere, a surface facing the Sun receives about 1.36 x 10^3 W on each square metre. This value is called the solar constant. The Earth-Sun distance is 1.5 x 10^11 m.
(a) State what the solar constant measures.
(b) How much power falls on a 5 m^2 solar collector facing the Sun in space?
(c) Write the formula linking the solar constant to the Sun's luminosity.
(d) Roughly what is the Sun's luminosity?
questions.answer: (a) The solar constant measures the solar energy received per second per unit area on a surface facing the Sun just outside the atmosphere. (b) Power = S x area = 1.36 x 10^3 x 5 = 6.8 x 10^3 W (6800 W). (c) L = S x 4 pi r^2. (d) Substituting gives L about 3.8 x 10^26 W.
questions.explanation: Definition; 6800 W; L = S x 4 pi r^2; ~3.8 x 10^26 W.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
Astronomers measure the distance to a nearby star by observing its parallax - the small apparent shift of the star against the background as the Earth orbits the Sun. A certain star shows a parallax angle of 0.2 arc-second.
(a) Define the parsec.
(b) Calculate the distance to this star in parsecs.
(c) Convert this distance to light years (1 pc = 3.26 ly).
(d) Why is the light year a unit of distance and not of time?
questions.answer: (a) A parsec is the distance at which 1 AU subtends an angle of 1 arc-second (1 pc = 3.086 x 10^16 m). (b) d = 1/p = 1/0.2 = 5 parsec. (c) 5 x 3.26 = 16.3 light years. (d) A light year is the distance light travels in one year; since it measures how far light goes, it is a unit of length, not of duration.
questions.explanation: Parsec definition; d = 1/p = 5 pc; 16.3 ly; light year = distance travelled by light.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
A massive star, about 15 times the mass of the Sun, has fused elements in its core all the way up to iron. Within a second its core collapses and the star explodes brilliantly, briefly rivalling the light of a whole galaxy. A tiny, extremely dense object is left at the centre.
(a) Why does the collapse begin once the core is made of iron?
(b) What is the brilliant explosion called?
(c) Name two possible remnants left behind and state what decides which one forms.
(d) What is the Chandrasekhar limit?
questions.answer: (a) Iron fusion absorbs energy rather than releasing it, so the core can no longer support itself against gravity and collapses. (b) The explosion is a SUPERNOVA. (c) The remnant may be a NEUTRON STAR (core about 1.4 to 3 solar masses) or a BLACK HOLE (core above about 3 solar masses); the remnant's MASS decides which forms. (d) The Chandrasekhar limit is the maximum mass of a white dwarf, about 1.4 solar masses.
questions.explanation: Iron cannot release fusion energy; supernova; neutron star or black hole by mass; Chandrasekhar limit ~1.4 M_sun.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
On a clear, dark night far from city lights a faint band of light stretches across the sky. This band is our own galaxy seen from the inside. It is a flattened, rotating system of a few hundred billion stars with a central bulge and spiral arms.
(a) Name this galaxy.
(b) What type of galaxy is it?
(c) Explain why we see it as a faint band of light.
(d) Name the two other main types of galaxy in Hubble's classification.
questions.answer: (a) It is the MILKY WAY. (b) It is a SPIRAL galaxy. (c) We are inside the flattened disc, so looking along the plane of the disc we see the combined light of its many distant stars as a faint milky band. (d) The other two main types are ELLIPTICAL and IRREGULAR galaxies.
questions.explanation: Milky Way; spiral; disc seen edge-on from inside; elliptical and irregular.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
In 1965 two scientists detected a faint microwave 'hiss' coming from every direction in the sky, at a temperature of about 2.7 K. This radiation, together with the observed recession of galaxies and the proportion of hydrogen and helium in the universe, forms the main evidence for a leading cosmological theory.
(a) Name the theory.
(b) What is the faint microwave radiation called?
(c) Give the two other lines of evidence mentioned in the passage.
(d) What does the 2.7 K radiation represent?
questions.answer: (a) The theory is the BIG BANG theory. (b) The radiation is the COSMIC MICROWAVE BACKGROUND (CMB). (c) The other evidence is the EXPANSION of the universe (recession of galaxies / Hubble's law) and the ABUNDANCE of light elements (about 75% hydrogen, 25% helium). (d) It represents the cooled-down afterglow of the hot, dense early universe.
questions.explanation: Big Bang; CMB; expansion and light-element abundance; cooled afterglow of the early universe.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
Edwin Hubble found that distant galaxies recede from us, and that a galaxy's recession velocity is proportional to its distance. This relation, v = H0 d, underlies the idea of an expanding universe. Take H0 = 70 km/s per Mpc.
(a) State Hubble's law in words.
(b) A galaxy is 120 Mpc away; find its recession velocity.
(c) Another galaxy recedes at 10500 km/s; find its distance.
(d) How is 1/H0 useful?
questions.answer: (a) The recession velocity of a galaxy is directly proportional to its distance from us. (b) v = H0 x d = 70 x 120 = 8400 km/s. (c) d = v / H0 = 10500 / 70 = 150 Mpc. (d) 1/H0 gives a rough estimate of the age of the universe (about 13.8 billion years).
questions.explanation: Law in words; v = 8400 km/s; d = 150 Mpc; 1/H0 estimates the age.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
Two stars, P and Q, appear equally bright in the night sky. Careful measurements show that star P is 10 light years away, while star Q is 100 light years away. Brightness falls off as the inverse square of distance.
(a) Which star is intrinsically more luminous, and why?
(b) What is the difference between apparent brightness and luminosity?
(c) If Q were moved to the same distance as P, how would its brightness compare with P's?
(d) What does a star's colour tell us about it?
questions.answer: (a) Star Q is far more luminous. Although both look equally bright, Q is ten times farther, and brightness falls as 1/distance^2; to appear as bright from ten times the distance, Q must emit about 100 times more energy per second. (b) Apparent brightness is how bright a star looks from Earth (it depends on distance); luminosity is the star's true total power output, independent of distance. (c) At the same distance as P, Q would appear about 100 times brighter than P. (d) A star's colour indicates its surface temperature - blue-white is hottest, red is coolest.
questions.explanation: Q more luminous (inverse-square); apparent vs true output; Q would be ~100x brighter; colour = temperature.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
The Sun is a middle-aged star made almost entirely of hydrogen and helium. It has a layered structure, and different processes carry energy from its core to its surface, from where it finally escapes as sunlight. Occasionally dark, cooler patches appear on its bright surface.
(a) Name the layer where the Sun's energy is generated.
(b) Name the visible surface and the dark patches on it.
(c) Name the faint outer atmosphere seen during a total solar eclipse.
(d) State the two main gases that make up the Sun.
questions.answer: (a) Energy is generated in the CORE by nuclear fusion. (b) The visible surface is the PHOTOSPHERE; the dark, cooler patches are SUNSPOTS. (c) The faint outer atmosphere seen at a total eclipse is the CORONA. (d) The Sun is made mainly of HYDROGEN and HELIUM.
questions.explanation: Core; photosphere and sunspots; corona; hydrogen and helium.
